items.body:
Written for four Ebow-ed guitars, 'Avaeken' preserves a site-specific piece that O'Malley used to accompany an exhibition by Banks Violette. It's a microtonal symphony dedicated to Alvin Lucier and Kali Malone that's almost physically disorienting - RIYL Eleh, Phill Niblock, Pauline Oliveros et al.

It must be difficult to strike a balance when you're best known for creating some of the heaviest, most chest-pummeling drone music to ever vibrate from a stack of Sun amplifiers. But O'Malley's risen to the challenge; 'Avaeken' is relatively minimal, for him at least, but smacks with an intensity that you don't really see coming until your body starts feeling it. Made using four vibrating strings, he tunes the instruments to create that unsettling beating sound that seems to whirl around the noggin as the resonances interfere with each other. O'Malley wrote the piece following a commission from Belgium's ZWERM electric guitar quartet in 2020, performing it a handful of times before they knuckled down and recorded it in Gent's Muziekcentrum De Bijloke, a medieval hospital that's been fitted out with the proper acoustic treatments. 

And if you've been studying O'Malley's output carefully, you'll already know that he's frequently been spotted alongside Violette, the American artist best known for his huge sculptures and installations. The two have been friends for two decades at this point and have worked together multiple times, so when Violette was describing his show 'Wish You Were Here', an exhibition that tears at the fabric of America's subcultural underground, O'Malley immediately thought about this piece. The link might not be obvious, but O'Malley's use of phase cancellation - when "sound energy is eating itself", in O'Malley's own words - reaps ample rewards here. The effect is unsubtle, penetrating oscillations so disorienting that Violette's themes of societal rot emanate from every skewed tone.

O'Malley presents two takes of the same piece, fixing Violette's striking artwork - of a cracked mirror ball - to the cover. And it's incredible to hear him working as a composer for a change, letting the ZWERM quartet do the heavy lifting. Their expertise helps elevate the piece; it's precise, expertly rendered gear, the kind of thing you need to give your full attention to. Surprisingly, it's also got more in common with those Sunn O))) records than you might expect - play at high volume and you'll know exactly what we mean.

items.body:
Probably the biggest curveball in rap since Lil’ Bs ‘Rain In England’, Cities Aviv lands on Black Truffle with a set of psilocybin-infused dream sequences influenced by Jandek. Strange but true!​

Sticking out like a sore thumb next to Black Truffle’s usual lineup of avant, jazz, minimalist and electroacoustic pioneers and mavericks, Cities Aviv is the work of Wilbert Gavin Mays, who also records as African-American Sound Recordings, squeezing hip-hop conventions thru a chopped and screwed haze of “hermetic décollage”packed with fuzzy ambient interludes, loopy clouded reflections and stream-of-consciousness bars. 

Gavin Mays has always been on the perimeter of many scenes, happy enough to draw his own landscape while everyone else churned up the same old mud. That's truer than ever on his recent run, culminating in this brilliantly unexpected Black Truffle co-sign. Operating on his lonesome, Mays creates music that can't be pigeonholed - it's barely even rap. He spits on the two-part title track, but his words dilate awkwardly over noisy, new age synths and blown-out, pitch-screwed rhythms. They might not even be strictly on the beat at all, a mood that he prolongs throughout 'Even Colder Spring’, an album that in places sounds more like Seefeel than it does MF DOOM.

While Mays’ work can sometimes read claustrophobically bleak, the production here is surprisingly approachable; the instrumental ‘Martine Drift’ could almost be a snatch of Cluster’s Zuckerzeit caught through dial-up internet, and the distant drums of ‘L_area’ cross with lo-fi IDM, while closer ‘Final Heaven’ dissolves a cloud of loops thru almost seven minutes of ecstatic, rippling distortion. And as the label point out, the cover art is inspired by Jandek’s Corwood Industries label, which gives you some idea of where it's at.

items.body:
Roland Kayn, Marino Zuccheri, Coro da Camera della RAI, Roma, and Nino Antonellini's "Kayn: Cybernetics III / Nono: Contrappunto dialettico alla mente (Avantgarde Vinyl Series)" via Deutsche Grammophon.

"Luigi Nono (1924–1990) was widely celebrated for his entire career. A central figure in post-war serialism, the Venetian composer emerged during the 1950s as one third of the “avant-garde trinity”, alongside Karlheinz Stockhausen and Pierre Boulez.

“Contrappunto” was composed for 2-channel magnetic tape in 1968, during a period when Nono was deeply committed to the international student struggles, as well as opposition to the Vietnam War. In basing the work on an early 17th century madrigal-comedy by Adriano Banchieri, Nono explained that he was “seeking to reflect the type of musical process used by Banchieri: the focus on the voice, introduction of sound material of the time, humorous and parodic distortion especially in the lyrical and dramatic elements … but in today’s actuality”

Roland Kayn’s Cybernetics III poignantly anticipates advancements in synthesis, computing and recording technology, as well as the development of samplers and sequencers. How these tools would be embraced by generations of artists who followed in Kayn’s wake, entirely re-formed the frameworks of electronic music. As such, Cybernetics III anticipated vast shifts in creative thinking.

Mastered & cut from the original analogue ¼ inch 2-track master tapes by Rainer Maillard and Sidney Claire Meyer at Emil Berliner Studios."

items.body:
Following 2024's avant-prog-Americana song cycle 'Viewfinder', guitar deity Wendy Eisenberg goes chamber pop on their self-titled latest, tipping their hat to Judee Sill, Gillian Welch, Van Dyke Parks and Joanna Newsom.

When they relocated from rural Western Mass to Brooklyn in 2020, Eisenberg was hit with a wave of longing for the open landscape they'd left behind. They were drawn to classic country and folk records, perfectly poised offerings from Willie Nelson and John Hartford and lavish pop-folk records from Jimmy Webb and Van Dyke Parks as well as the weirdo fare of Richard Dawson et al. So when 'Viewfinder', a way of deconstructing the experience following eye surgery in 2011, was finished, Eisenberg started writing "genuinely folk songs" and swapping out their usually showy, complex performance for a form of relative simplicity that they explain is inherently strange all the same. Prog becomes folk, basically. And they're not on their own; more eaze handles the lush string arrangements, playing pedal steel and synthesizer, and a loose band forms around that axis, with drummer Ryan Sawyer and bassist Trevor Dunn.

But despite the personnel, it's resolutely Eisenberg's album. Their voice sounds unrestrained, capturing the era they're referencing and their own emotional (and physical upheaval). It's fragile but strangely warm on the country-tinged Jim O'Rourke-like 'Will You Dare' and hypnotic on the baroque 'Meaning Business', a track they wrote in the wake of David Lynch's death as the antithesis of the "Lynchian" aesthetic. And they should really get their flowers for this one; Americana, especially now, is teetering on a precipice, almost knocked off the edge by half-assed, churned attempts and underwritten pastiches. Eisenberg's an attentive listener and someone who's surrounded themself with similarly sensitive ears, people who are able to fill their heart and their sound so what we hear is as byzantine as a Gastr del Sol record but sounds as effortless as John Prine's 'Angel From Montgomery'. If you loved Joanna Newsom's 'Ys' and have never found anything quite as satisfying, this is the one.

items.body:
HTRK slickly seduce with the unheimlich sensuality on 'Work (Work, Work)', on a new pressing for 2026.

While it may be gauche to attribute the lightless mood of this LP to the departure of Sean Stewart in 2010, it certainly lends some inescapable context. It's hardly like HTRK were doing tween-pop previously, but the sense of gloom and dystopia is almost suffocatingly closer to the edge, from the crawling-on-all-fours pacing, to the detached, androgynous vocals of Jonnine Standish and their perversely detailed production values.

They've got our attention instantly with the sideroom synth eurotica of 'Ice Eyes Eis', and sustain the mood beautifully into the pinging metallic delays and seeping reverb of 'Slo Go', sounding like Atelecine produced by a young Geoff Barrow after a Birthday Party binge. Dragging us further down into the abyss, on 'Eat Yr Heart' the drums become clammier while Jonnine's vocals drift like ghostly vapour trail. At the album's apex, 'Skinny', the beats feel like a dystrophied version of something from Mika Vainio's 'Life, It Eats You Up…' album, and 'Synthetik' serves a tangibly textured taste of steely Techno pulses and opiated post-punk guitar drifts into 'Poison'.

To close, the atmopshere weighs heavier still on 'Work That Body', tracing anaesthetic connections with their Melbourne forefathers, Pelican Daughters, before the bleak romance of 'Love Triangle' and the blank-eyed writhe of 'Body Double'.

For fans of occluded sonics from Pump to Atelecine or Mika Vainio, it's as good as it gets.

items.body:
Stefan Betke aka Pole’s holy trilogy of frayed dub experiments resurfaces for a 20th anniversary reissue, taking us back to smokey nights at the turn of the century and some of the finest post basic-channel dub echoes ever released. Essential listening if you’re into anything from Rhythm & Sound to Vainqueuer, Jon Hassell to Jackie Mittoo.

As legend goes, Pole took his name from a malfunctioning Waldorf 4-Pole filter which produced hisses and pops which weren’t really controllable or predictable, much like a living organism. Betke realised the potential and came to alchemically morph and render them with judicious FX dubbing into a groundbreaking sort of minimalist electro-dub that sounds exceedingly good with a spliff and glass of booze. Working somewhere between the variants of abstract techno on Chain Reaction and Mille Plateaux’s cutting edge minimalist strains, Pole’s first trio of albums inarguably helped lay the foundations for dub techno as it’s come to be known and are held in the highest regard by practically everyone who owns them. 

The Pole aesthetic is patently laid out in ‘1’, where his organic clicks ’n pops come out to play accompanied by lilting organ and jazzy bass channelling Jackie Mittoo via Jon Hassell and Rhythm & Sound into a uniquely, gauzy, gaseous state. But for us, his sound really comes into its own on ‘2’, where the opening melodica motif still sends electric shivers down the spine and opens out into the kind of sculpted, layered dub bass that spawned dubstep, and flows out into myriad, mesmerising permutations, but this time swapping out the hazy licks for a cavernous, brooding melancholy (that really matched this moody teenager’s psyche at the time) and reverberated through into the more humid, drizzly and funereal atmosphere conjured in the equally spellbinding spectral dub metaphysics of ‘3’.

So strong was the impact of these albums on the late ‘90s underground, they even generated a “pastiche” that was unwittingly issued (and subsequently deleted) by Fat Cat on their split series, but was purportedly made by V/Vm in a snidey but frankly hilarious prank, albeit one that demonstrates just how ubiquitous and influential Betke’s sound was at the time. More than that, it’s fair to say the 20 year cycle hasn’t rinsed out the appeal of this triptych one bit; it remains one of electronic music’s most enigmatic and strangely moving, tactile bodies of work.

items.body:
Lushest, subtropically-infused jazz lilt by seasoned Chicago musicians who’ve worked with SZA, Whitney, Lil Nas X and Clairo, between them - all stamped with International Anthem’s seal of approval and with the pirates of Milton Nascimiento and Herbie Hancock in its breezy air. Record of the summer..?

“album notes by Josh Terry: Imagine it’s late afternoon, you’re outside by the lake, and there’s sunlight on the water. This is the peaceful and contemplative scene that Matt Gold and Resavoir set on their collaborative LP Horizon. Across 10 lush and exploratory tracks, it’s the product of two Chicago-based musicians—Will Miller, the acclaimed trumpeter, composer, and producer who’s worked with SZA, Whitney, and more, and Gold, a seasoned multi-instrumentalist and accomplished guitarist—effortlessly combining their distinct sensibilities for something hypnotic and tangibly inviting. What started as a love letter to their shared admiration for ‘60s and ‘70s Brazilian music evolved into a dynamic and sprawling body of work. These sunny and expansive tunes are as immersive as they are endlessly replayable.

Both Miller and Gold attended Oberlin College’s Conservatory of Music together and in the years after graduating, they orbited each other around Chicago’s music communities. “We were showing up for each other as friends and taking an interest in each other's projects, noticing a lot of resonances and similarities working within in our music,” says Gold, who’s collaborated with artists like Makaya McCraven and Jamila Woods and stretched the bounds of jazz and Americana on solo albums Imagined Sky and Midnight Choir. “We had talked so much about eventually working together that it was almost like an ongoing bit at a certain point,” says Miller. Though they had known each other for over a decade, they first had their chance on “Inside Minds,” the breezy lead single on 2023’s Resavoir. While those sessions were remote, two had palpable chemistry.

It wasn’t until Miller left the touring band of the Chicago group Whitney in 2023 that their plans to make music together in person came to fruition. “When I first started Resavoir, I was chasing the desire to produce records and now that I had time to focus exclusively on that, Matt was the first person I called to come to the studio,” says Miller. The two had bonded over an admiration for the Brazilian guitarist Luis Bonfa and songwriter Milton Nascimento, especially the latter’s work with Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter, so they decided to use nylon string guitar as a starting point for these early sessions. “Canopy,” which opens Horizon, was the earliest track. Kicking off with bright acoustic chords, the song slowly unfurls into a slinking groove, samples, and fluttering leads from soprano saxophonist Tim Bennett.

As these initial experiments proved successful, Gold and Miller felt they could broaden the scope of their vision. “We were initially conceiving of it as this acoustic guitar driven record but eventually we wanted to frame it orchestrally and see how many shades and colors we can bring in around that sound,” says Gold. “Dewy” thrives within this orchestral palette of woozy synths, strings from Macie Stewart, Claire Chenette’s oboe, flautist Wills McKenna, and French horns from Lloyd Billingham. “We discovered that our multi-instrumentalist mentalities—using piano and bass, samplers, drum grooves, guitar ideas all as starting points— nurtured the broad orchestration across this record,” says Miller.

“The LP took about a year with on-and-off sessions,” says Miller. “The songs benefit from letting them ferment for a couple months, coming back to it, and seeing what sort of new flavors have developed.” Co-produced by Miller and Gold (and mixed by Dave Vettraino), Horizon proudly reflects the artists’ vast artistic community and musical network in Chicago and beyond. Along with Gold, Eddie Burns (Clairo), Peter Mannheim (Tony Glausi), and Carter Lang (SZA, Lil Nas X) provide drums and percussion throughout. On the dreamlike single “Diversey Beach,” New York songwriter Mei Semones lends vocals and along with her band members Noah Leong and Claudius Agrippa, collaborated on a mesmerizingly conversational string arrangement. “We wrote "Diversey Beach" on the coldest day of the year watching a blizzard coming down out of the window, where the sounds of the cars driving by sounded like waves crashing on a beach,” says Miller. “I sent it to Mei Semones, who I’ve been a fan of for a long time. She's absolutely incredible and it’s amazing what she did with it.”

Horizon is a testament to the feeling of endless possibilities that come from collaboration. It’s a remarkable synthesis of two artists who share musical community and an artist lineage but have carved their own paths in unique ways. Nowhere is this more evident than “Hazel Canyon,” which boasts Gold’s silky pedal steel and a subtly enveloping arrangement that evokes Erasmo Carlos. “Musically, we're always trying to capture a fleeting moment of infinite expanse, feeling the vastness of things while knowing they'll always change,” says Gold. “This record keeps the light reflecting on the water just a little longer -- our collaborative process running through the backbone of these songs and rippling out in so many beautiful directions..””

items.body:
Oh man this is almost too much - just wall to wall genius in action courtesy of Floating Points & Eliot Bernard's Melodies International label -  spotlightling fire in the crown of Mad Professor’s pivotal London Lovers Rock and dub stable, Ariwa Sounds: from an immense monk-steppa ‘Non Violence Dub’ ft. Horace Andy, thru the Motown soul-infused Lovers of Davina Stone on 'Silly Wasn’t I’, to a Kofi gem recently found on Moin’s street-soul/digidub mix, the ruffneck charge of Mafia & Fluxy ‘6 Million Dub’, early Wild Bunch styles on Aisha’s ‘Can You Feel It’, and deadly ‘Liberated Woman’ voiced by Ranking Ann. All killer no filler!

“In 1979, Neil Fraser (artistically known as Mad Professor) founded Ariwa Sounds, the longest-serving and one of the most influential independently owned Reggae studios and record labels in the UK. From humble beginnings set up in the front room of Neil's home in South London recording on 4-track and homemade equipment, Ariwa would go on to record and release over 300 albums including works from some of the most impactful and storied artists of their time in the genres of Reggae, Dub, and Lovers Rock

Whilst our previous release in collaboration with Ariwa captured the label's early sound, a shared performance with Neil in Osaka and regular visits to his South London studio inspired us to assemble this 15-track compilation, showcasing the label's output across 45 years. Our release emphasizes some of the label's greatest vocalists: Johnny Clarke, Sandra Cross, Kofi, U Roy, Sister Nancy, Queen Omega, Aisha, Garnett Cross, Abel Miller, Horace Andy and more — presenting the Motown and Stax influences in the Lovers Rock, but also provides a glimpse into the dubbier and more experimental side of the label, showcasing Ariwa's commitment to quality but also their personality, philosophy and their humour. Love songs, break-up songs, socially engaged songs, dub experimentations — this compilation is not a "best of" Ariwa but a diverse and honest celebration of the label through the lens of Melodies International.”

Curated by Rosa Pistola, 'Dioses Tribales' surveys Mexico's tribal landscape, placing scene architects like Javier Estrada, Ricardo Reyna, DJ Mouse, DJ Tetris and Dj Morphius alongside beatmakers who are steering its current course, such as "TEKTRIBAL" innovator Freebot and Monterrey's Clap Freckles.

Pistola continues her "Tribal Sound System" project with this tight, tidy selection; rewind a few weeks and you'll remember 'Incorrigible', her latest album that built a sequence of rickety, hard-swung club tracks on the foundations of Mexico's tribal sound. 'Dioses Tribales' is a companion piece in a sense, providing a way for Pistola to pay her respects to the scene's pioneers and also highlight her contemporary peers - basically, it's an invaluable (and very digestible) line in to a movement that's far too often misunderstood outside of Mexico. The first vibrations were felt back in the early 2000s, when producers in Monterrey and Mexico City began to define their own sound as American house and techno flooded local clubs. Back then, you could wander round any city center and hear local bands playing indigenous music on pan flutes, shakers and traditional drums. And it was Ricardo Reyna, on 2005's 'Danza Azteca', who was the first artist to integrate these elements into his forward-thinking productions. This track's the reason it was labeled tribal prehispánico music in the first place, in fact.

Fittingly, Pistola opens the compilation with three of tribal's key artists. Reyna provides a sequel to his milestone, 'Danza Azteca II (El baile de los Dioses)', a track that shows the development that's happened in the last two decades, spicing up the central 4/4 kick with vocal chants, clattering rhythms and an urgent, driving bassline. And then Pistola puts the spotlight on tribal guarachero, the sound that emerged as artists began to fold in rhythms from Cumbia and other Afro-Cuban and Afro-Spanish dances. Manu Morales, aka DJ Mouse, is one of the most conspicuous early visionaries in this respect - his sunny 2005 breakout 'Folklore' is still one of the genre's touchstones. And he appears here with another nod to the Caribbean, muddling reggaetón's ubiquitous 'Dem Bow' rhythm, repurposed from Shabba Ranks' 1991 anthem, with EDM stabs and clanking pan drums. Oaxaca's DJ Tetris, meanwhile, was responsible for shaping tribal costeño, notoriously defining the sound on that epic 'N.A.A.F.I Tribal' compilation from 2014. His 'Rumbea Conmigo' is a collaboration with DJ Giovanni Rios that shows how, in the coastal south, tribal fused with Mariachi music, using synths to replace the accordions.

And it wouldn't be proper if there wasn't an appearance from Javier Estrada. Estrada didn't invent tribal prehispánico, but you could say he perfected it - just peep his 2014 album of the same name. And that's where Pistola pulls 'Guerrero Azteca' from. It's arguably one of the genre's affecting tracks, packed out with animalistic growls, deep, pounding rhythms and ASMR-ready rainforest sounds that seem to have directly inspired Pistola's own productions. And over on German netlabel KUMBALE a year later, Alfonso Luna released his own 'TRIBAL PREHISPANICO' treatise, referencing its potent cocktail of percussive dings and vocal snippets with the brilliant 'Bakalao'. The contemporary charge then is led by Pistola's production partner FREEBOT who displays how modern techniques have shaped his razor-sharp, Berghain-ready "TEKTRIBAL" sound on 'Ela toma (Dioses tribales)' and Clap Freckles, who made his name producing cheeky bootlegs and edits, and impresses with his hypnotic exclusive 'Los Dioses Tribales (Deja fluir)'.

We can't think of a better way to get acquainted with tribal's past, present and future - even the cover, showing the genre's notorious pointed boots, is iconic. You know what to do.

items.body:
The latest from A Colourful Storm’s Fleetway Tapes sublabel comes from Tokyo-based selector, composer and NTS resident Abiu, mining an hour of mostly Japanese prog, no wave and avant-industrial nuggets, floating into spoken word, free jazz and fringe dubs that’ll make you wonder where the hell she finds her tunes. If you've chewed up the Concentric Circles mixes on Berceuse Heroique and exhausted Blackest Ever Black’s ‘Id Mud’ mixtape series - this one’s for you.

One of those tapes you have to sink deep into rather than a casual dip, 'It's the Rest of a Stump' is packed to the gills with unclassifiable fire - avant oddities that are far too deep for any algorithm. Abiu will be a familiar name if you've scraped around the edges of the NTS schedule where her regular transmissions betray her vast knowledge; a show where you can find lesser-known art rock next to scrappy outsider techno, EBM and synthwave, Japanese folk sandwiched between spoken word and modern jazz sides. How she finds any of it, we're not sure, but it's the kind of gear that will inevitably lead to lengthy Discogs sessions - we guarantee it. 

So she's a lifer, for sure. And that's exactly the kind of feeling you get when you sit through this one. There's no need to go track to track because the individual elements aren't really why it works - it's the expedition that Abiu takes you on, harking back to a time when digging hadn't been so sanitised by bait algorithms and “released on this day xx years ago” campaigns. For an hour, we're dropped into a musty back room leafing through used bins and racks of tapes, searching through newsgroups and blogs - finding loose threads and wormholes and following them to albums that are prob 95% shit with just a few short minutes of glory buried inside. Abiu's done the work for us basically.

And if you want some added credentials, Abiu is also a researcher at Saidera Ai Design, the acoustics wing of Saidera Mastering, the team that just restored and remastered Miles Davis's catalog. 

Whewwww!

items.body:
French cold wave and goth disco par excellence. Not hard to imagine Annie Hogan spinning the likes of ‘L’Appel Du Froid’ at The Batcave, or insouciant, kohl-eyed Gallic teens bopping at their local goth jamboree to this lot. Evidently there’s clear reasons why this DIY self-release of ’88 now trades for triple figures on resale markets…

“Opéra de Nuit emerge from their long slumber to grace Dark Entries with the frostiest of reissues. Formed in 1982 in Valréas in the southeast of France, Opéra de Nuit only released 3 records throughout their career: EPs in 1984 and 1986, with a full LP following in 1988. But devotees of dark music will need no introduction to this band, who are almost definitional of the coldwave genre, and whose rabid cult following has each record readily trading for three-digit prices. Opéra de Nuit’s sound is pure hellish heaven: frigid synths, jangly guitars, and sorrow-laden vox. 

Check out the pummelling desperation of “Annabella,” the uber-brooding vibes of “Boris Transylvania Camp,” or the elegant anthem “Karen Lloyd” (and don’t forget to watch the video!). This reissue collects their entire newly remastered discography – thirteen lucky tracks. This reissue marks the first time that their work will be reissued on vinyl and digital, and is presented in gatefold jacket with lyrics and photos. Whether you’re new to the genre or a veteran of the coldest waves, Opéra de Nuit brings the essential sound of immortal despair.”

FELT capture deep & mysterious activities for posterity with a double bill from someone called bushes (no clues!) and scene veteran Klaus, recorded and mixed by Murray Collier (aka Dip Friso, Grim Lusk) in Glasgow, 2024. Trust there’s oodles of intrigue & stuff inside.

Always encouraging when music has no immediate frames of reference, RIYL’s or FFO’s, and this lot do it very fucking well, operating at a sort of eyes-at-half-mast tempo and headspace that’s neither ambient nor primed for the club, like some kinda holding music between modes of existence (we didn’t say liminal lol), full of dank atmosphere and the promise of whatever the night has in store. 

If the A side gives a whiff of isolation, the flip is all dusk and romance, snatches of saxophone drifting off in the distance with bass pulses and endless delay sending us to an unintelligible, beautiful place.

One of those tapes we guarantee you’ll rinse endlessly, we’ve had it on a loop for a couple of hours and trust it casts a fucking spell.

items.body:
Ezra Feinberg’s third album Soft Power sees the composer-guitarist enlist an impressive array of fellow musicians including Mary Lattimore, David Moore (Bing & Ruth), Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, and Robbie Lee.

"Defined by its abundance of melodies, repeating figures and ecstatic improvisations, Soft Power exudes an enlightened and transformative spirit to empower the listener. The compassionate, tender-hearted opener ‘Future Sand’ deftly interweaves flutes and steady arpeggios. The Reichian pulse beneath the soaring melody is played not on the customary analogue sequencer, but on finger-picked acoustic guitar, one of the lodestars of Feinberg’s compositional approach. ‘Soft Power’, the buoyant and mesmeric title track that follows builds over a rich bed of guitars and a reverb-y Rhodes melody reminiscent of a Strata East LP, its narrative arc bountiful in energy, optimism and future dreaming, a perfect accompaniment to long days of summertide.

‘Pose Beams’ blends the chamber-jazz approach of Penguin Café Orchestra with a balletic kosmische, climaxing with a galvanising crescendo and “free improv” section performed by fellow New Yorkers - Robbie Lee (piano) and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, whose granular and modular synths sprinkle particle dust over the expressive drumming of John Thayer. ‘Flutter Intensity’ evokes in part the music of Cluster as played on acoustic guitars, which ping-pong across the stereo field, providing the canvas for a plaintive vibraphone line reminiscent of TNT-era Tortoise. Instruments move in tandem, but also drift and glide allowing them the space to hang in the air, the variegated rhythms, textures, and tones all laced into the fabric of the album.

At the centrefold of the albums 7-tracks is ‘The Big Clock’, a tryptic piece that evolves from pairs of stretched varying tones, creating fields of technicolour over an unabashed motorik beat, serving to offset the pastoral and ambient registers heard elsewhere. It features the first of two appearances from David Moore (Bing & Ruth) who plays lilting piano lines on the come-down. ‘There Was Somebody There’ returns to the album’s earlier wistfulness, a hard stereo-panned soundworld with lightly strummed, interlocking acoustic guitars combining to pigment a washy, painterly scene. David Moore and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma provide reviving synths, the underlying pulse that seems to simulate a life cycle; another day on Earth. The album closes with the reflective ‘Get Some Rest’ featuring Mary Lattimore, whose harp pluckings set a dreamlike tone against bare organic acoustics and flourishing flutes to create a sense of realignment and restoration.

Feinberg artfully transcends the listener to an enriched place, his compositions distinguished by the deep humanity that lies at their core, plugging the listener into a state of wide eyed being, open and alive. Soft Power then is Ezra’s own mantra but also one of power giving - a colourful catharsis translated into music. Feinberg’s music always speaks to the listener, but Soft Power, in whispering, speaks loudest."

Suzanne Ciani’s ‘gay male’ alter ego Steve with a 1982 foray into peak time wavey business, including that coca cola bottle opening sound she did the sound design for plus a pitched down vocal from Ciani and a cameo from Peter Baumann of Tangerine Dream, followed by a killer slice of filtered House  ‘Steve Saves the World’ and a crazy, ‘Home Of The Brave’ style linndrum closer “Steve Happy Birthday Wishes”. Crazy find!

"Legendary composer, sound designer, and Buchla maestra Suzanne Ciani has a staggering list of accolades and accomplishments, from scoring Hollywood films to releasing influential new age records to literally designing the Coca-Cola bottle-opening sound. In the late 70s/early 80s, Ciani, while living in New York, acquired an Eventide H 949 harmonizer, which offered high fidelity pitch-shifting. In her words, “When I adjusted the pitch of my voice to 0.80, my natural voice became re-invented as what was clearly a gay man, who I called Steve. I became Steve; and Steve expressed himself as only he could.” Ciani adopted the male persona and collaborated with Peter Baumann of Tangerine Dream on “Steve Goes to a Party.” The track features Ciani-as-Steve adlibbing in decadent and delirious fashion alongside Baumann’s robotically funky beats.

Steve would emerge again a few years later at George Louvis’s Stardust Studios in New Jersey, to create “Steve Saves the World,” an absurdist and ecstatic proto-house groover complete with a gospel-esque chorus from the Stardust All-Stars. This EP is rounded out by a birthday wish to Ciani’s then-boyfriend Alfred on “Steve Happy Birthday Wishes” featuring Suzanne. Steve’s Out of the Closet perfectly captures the delirious techno-poptimism of the 1980s downtown avant-garde, with parallels in Robert Ashley’s Perfect Lives or Lynn Goldsmith’s project Will Powers, responsible for the track “Adventures in Success.” The Steve sleeve was designed by Eloise Shir-Juen Leigh, and the record also includes a birthday card with liner notes from Ciani."

30 year return of Model 500’s overlooked but killer comet, straddling classic late ‘80s and emergent ‘90s strands of deep 313 electro-techno.

One of the more distant stars in the Metroplex galaxy, Juan Atkins’ 1993 single tends to the more introspective, wide-eyed side of Detroit club music. ‘I See The Light’ places his signature over-the-shoulder vocoder in an aerodynamic answer to his late ‘80s electro classics, riddled with ‘Clear’-styled arps and wickedly woozy choral pads ideal for tempering a set between more boisterous gear.

‘Pick Up the Flow’ is more clearly in step with the deep techno sound he was concocting at the time (often with Moritz Von Oswald), but still whirring with electro mechanics, balancing glyding pads and vocal soliloquy for the first half, and weaving in more Eastern-oriented melodic tang on the 2nd part.

Kurt Wagner's seventeeth album as Lambchop - drawing on gospel and centuries-old Scots-Appalachian call-and-response singing.

"Lambchop's seventeenth album Punching the Clown finds Kurt Wagner returning to first principles. Sparked by a late-night radio encounter with an unidentified gospel recording, Wagner fell deep into the world of "lined out singing" a centuries-old Scots-Appalachian call-and-response tradition in which a lone clerk leads a choir through hymns, word by unadorned word. That spirit of raw, communal voice shapes every moment of Punching the Clown: Wagner spent years studying great songwriters and relearning his craft from the ground up, whittling dozens of songs down to twelve. Recorded in three days with guitarist Andrew Broder, Justin Vernon on banjo, and a six-part choir assembled by Blake Morgan and engineered by Lambchop veteran Mark Nevers, the album is graceful, wry, and quietly devastating. Out August 21, 2026 on City Slang.

Produced by Ryan Olson and recorded August 25–27, 2025, at April Base, Wisconsin. The record was completed over three days and features Kurt Wagner (vocals), Andrew Broder (guitar), Justin Vernon (banjo), and a six-part vocal ensemble, with additional choir recordings in London and Minneapolis."

items.body:
Last spotted on A Good Year's 'Play', Texas-born singer, producer and multi-instrumentalist Riya Mahesh, aka Quiet Light, turns in the sequel to 2023's 'Blue Angel Sparkling Silver', mashing Imogen Heap's experimentation with The Postal Service's emo-friendly electro-pop.

There's a polish to 'Blue Angel Sparkling Silver 2', but Mahesh's production smarts don't ever overwhelm the music's emotional core. And although she plays fast and loose with the vocal effects, chopping, processing and layering her voice in much the same way Heap did when she inadvertently kickstarted cloud rap, it's still possibly to sense the human in the machine. It's a technique that's helped Mahesh get noticed recently; she appeared alongside Late Verlane on A Good Year's sublime album opener 'Dealerz' and the new mixtape sees her move to True Panther, labelmates with artists who share the same DNA: Glasser, Oklou and Lauren Auder, for example.

On 'Berlin', that seems as if it would be self-explanatory, she avoids the temptation to drape her song in techno finery, instead telling her story of over-indulgence with restraint, singing almost unaccompanied until her sparse drones are met by a simple breakbeat. Her voice is left to do the heavy lifting and it's up for the job; Mahesh is a gifted producer, sure, but as a singer she's able to really show her range, comfortably belting out power pop or existing in a more ambient space, like on 'New Dream'. She's even able to bridge the gap between electro pop and Surf Gang-style Soundcloud rap on 'Postinternetfame' - and the breathy 'New Girls' sounds like it was at least partially inspired by Burial. Nae bad at all.

items.body:
Roping in Pierre Bastien and Mark Cunningham to provide brass, Mike Cooper turns in his most kaleidoscopic fourth world dream sequence to date, drawing on dub and exotica to harmonise with Andrew Pekler's marooned soundscapes...

Cooper admits in the liner notes that although he's often compared with Jon Hassell, it's German painter Mati Klarwein fantastical album covers that always reminded him exactly why he was doing what he was doing. Because Cooper makes music for imaginary places, not tangible soundtracks but half dreamed, half lived experiences that course through his catalog of experiments. And his process has never been quite so vivid as it is on 'Stochastic Parrot', a suite of vertiginous reverberations that are struck through with Cooper's "real and virtual" lap steel twangs, collaged together from samples and field recordings that wobble like heat haze. 

Different pockets of rhythm bash into each other on 'ARCHAEOPTERYX', accompanied by Bastien and Cunningham's spiraling brass improvisations. And Cooper holds the sounds together with his lulling repeated phrases; the hand drums might sound as if they're in conflict with the cycling drum machine crashes, but that's the point - it's not like channeling a dream so much as it's like being subjected to three or four dreams simultaneously. It's the ghosts of jazz fusion being raked over coals at midnight: just tune into 'SUMATRA SAMPHIRE', with its distant animalistic wails and popcorn drums, or the granulized 'HAT YAI', that sounds like the prelude to a druggy ritual.

items.body:
Delicious debut vinyl of smouldering, dubwise downbeats by a Lithuanian artist hovering in the half light  somewhere between False Aralia’s dubwise pop pearls, Rhythm & Sound, and the knackered nocturnal musicks of ssabæ or Rat Heart.

Next up on Matthew Kent’s Short Span - the successor to Blowing Up the Workshop & Mana - is Marija Rasa aka emer’s dream sequence of crawl-pace slugs swaying on syrupy bass and sublimated to seductive vapours. For anyone paying closer attention, ‘Fog’ clearly reprises and expands on the elusive, smoky vibes felt on her 2024 digi drop for Stroom and in ’25 for Chicago’s Lillerne Tapes. However her sound is notably strapped with more supple layers of subbass and perfused with hands-on-desk dub tekkerz and a groggy spirit that really hits the spot for night owls or those chasing trip hop dragons.

‘Fog’ operates at the speed of slowed thought with seven cuts to sink right into. For half an hour she swaddles minds in high tog textures as tracks pass-out into hypnagogic bliss from the gentle descent into swole subs on ‘Below Altitude’, to gorgeous, spongiform bass and soul-grab chords of ‘Open’, and like Moritz Von oswald smelting his jazz trio back to Rhythm & Sound fundamentals in ‘Nobody Speaks’. A knack for eking out organic detail is most enchanting on the interplay of aerosolised thizz and massaged low end on ‘Room Five’, and leaves us levitating in the ssabæ-esque wooze to ‘The Evergreen Fog’ and hobbled, ghostly shape of ‘Calling’.

items.body:
Patricia Wolf's second Balmat album is the soundtrack to experimental filmmaker Edward Pack Davee's feature-length documentary 'Hrafnamynd', and mixes field recordings with AFX-esque lullaby themes, tape-mangled instrumental vamps and VHS-burn'd analog pads.

There's something oddly soothing about 'Hrafnamynd', and without seeing the documentary it's hard to know exactly why. Using film and digital, Davee recounts his childhood in Iceland through the volcanic island's ravens, exploring the landscape and folklore while scraping his own nostalgia. And Wolf's score attempts to mimic the surreal fusion of old and new by using her UDO Super 6, a powerful binaural analog-hybrid synth, to bring the past towards the present. "It has the ability to sound very modern," Wolf explains. "But can also sound so warm and fuzzy, like a synth from the 1970s." 

So we're treated to time-warped tracks like 'Early Memories', 'I Thought I Could Fly' and 'Hrafnaﬂing', the latter of which sounds as if it's an off-cut from Leila's 'Like Weather', and distressed, casual jams like 'Krummi's Theme' - the cue for the film's talking raven. But these are bounced against more self-consciously contemporary compositions; the glassy 'Huginn and Muninn', for example, or the balletic 'Surfing on Wind'. And the album's most generous track 'Echoes Through Time' reflects Wolf's full spectrum, distorting harmonies that settle into percussive sine chimes before disappearing into the distance.

Jahtari light the fuse on a bag of digidub sound system detonators by Jamaican producer Prince Riser, aka Robbie Reiser, ranging from low pressure skank to flying dread steppas and original vocal cuts by Sammy Gold & Madi Simmons, all heavily lathered in FX...

“Dub album full of sound system explosives by expert riddim tinkerer Prince Riser – hard rocking, spaced out Kawai synth digi bangers, hitting that sweet spot between analog and digital Reggae while drawing vibes from the legacy of Dread & Fred, Exterminator and Jammy.

Aside from the thunderous Dub epic “Through The Storm” Prince Riser’s debut LP is also featuring the killer vocal cuts “Poverty Ina Russia” by Sammy Gold – a super heavy depth charge of Sly & Robbie proportions – the soulful Wackie’s flavoured anthem “Keep On Trodding” by Madi Simmons (who sadly passed away in 2024) and the plonky digi stepper “Travelling Gal” by Prince Riser himself, each accompanied by a murderous Dub version.

With extra cosmic dust added by disrupt at the Jahtari home studio, “Through The Storm” is crucial gear for any sound system vinyl crate.”

items.body:
One of the most perfectly formed releases in Warp's vast catalogue, and arguably the most complete transmission from Drexciya's James Stinson (RIP).

One of James Stinson’s perfect storms bubbles up again on Warp after many years at the top of everyone’s wants list.  Originally issued as the 3rd Drexciyan Storm in 2001 - one year before Stinson’s death due to heart complications, on 3rd September, 2002 -  Lifestyles of the Laptop Café became an instant classic with Detroit house and techno lovers as well as for many listeners beyond that paradigm who were equally seduced by its sleek, louche arrangements and unforgettable tunes.

20+ years later it stands as a beautifully sore thumb in the Drexciyan catalogue; far more mellow, emotionally sublime than anything else produced during James Stinson’s too short tenure on this planet, framed by a neon glow which uniquely phosphoresces in the mind long after the needle hits the run-out. Nowadays it is justifiably elevated to the level of a peerless modern classic - a masterclass in sophisticated, futuristic electro-soul whose influence has only grown since its release, transcending time and space like few other records.

Under the title 東方不敗, meaning Invincible East, the record wraps an armoury of powerful percussion and native instrumentation around a narrative locus based on a swordsman character in a Jin Yong novel “who must make the ultimate sacrifice to attain knowledge and transform”. Coupled with the artist’s own observations on living in, and travelling around, Asia, it’s an urgent and gripping listen with a versatility and varied topography lending itself to DJ use and soundtracking industrial subterfuge alike.

日出東方 唯我不敗 starts out like ’05 sino grime or dubstep from a parallel dimension; Digital Properties trades in secretive choral code at a killer New Beta momentum which decelerates into the the wind-tunnel chug and pealing cyber-tribal chant of Esther. 

His signature triplets last heard on A Name Out Of Place wickedly come into play against sheer electric blue synth tone in King Of Hosts; we’re put thru an intense, Americanised club drill in Post-Soviet Models; and Torque Pulsations both literally and physically lives up to its name with a belly and spine-twysting EBM tattoo. 

 TIP!

items.body:
A Colourful Storm's Fleetway Tapes series follows classic entries from Time Is Away, Vladimir Ivkovic, Felix K, Young Sparks and others with a heart-stopping selection put together by Berlin-based film journo Florence Scott-Anderton, a fathoms-deep, laser-focused mix that doesn't come around often, engulfing high-art/low-culture TV samples with a series of cues excavated from film - think of it as a sort of Blockbuster Video nostalgia-tinted answer to Time Is Away's flawless thematic mixes.

Florence knows her shit. Not only does she provide words and sounds for MUBI's international film mag Notebook, where she's covered Tōru Takemitsu and crafted an ode to Derek Jarman, but she's a resident on NTS's ace Sounds on Screen. Nose through her archive and you'll find a deep dive into the sonics of lesbian cinema, an exploration of Aussie icon Nicole Kidman's filmography, a mix dedicated to Japanese vanguard Satoshi Kon, a history of the sounds of Iranian cinema and loads more (really, there's so much). And it's this same anti-hierarchal level of expertise and passion she brings to 'A Requiem for Prime Time', a very personal journey thru her memory banks that collages dialog samples, TV ambiance, art oddities and various soundtrack selections that eschew the usual narrative. We'll be honest, we've gotten pretty fatigued with the OST industrial complex and its parallel stream of repetitive, hyper-referential shovelcore outings from genre dorks whose interest in music peaked with 'Stranger Things'. Thankfully, Florence opts to sail down a completely different channel, not avoiding the mythologised synth wave completely (Simon Boswell's killer 'Hardware' cue 'It's Horrible... I Love It... What Is It?' shows up as a bonus like a peanut in caramel) but concentrating on dislocated, provocative and often completely overlooked sounds that drift far from the established "score bro" cult canon.

"It's not like you want to be an accountant," a muffled Australian voice narrates over ketamized SFX on the opening side. "You, like me, want something that is creative, that is out there a little bit." A clip from Peter Mullan's 2002 drama 'The Magdalene Sisters' appears, pulling us right back to that moment when trip-hop aesthetics bled into Hollywood's mainstream, and before long we’re riding a different train of thought, stitching cavernous twee rock with pastoral post-Glass minimalism and scratchy, evocative environmental recordings. Canned sax solos and airy guitar plucks fade into cuts from Mike Figgis's notorious experimental film 'Timecode', and somehow Woijciech Kilar's end credits from Francis Ford Copolla's 'Bram Stoker's Dracula' show up for some thematic relief. On the flip, Florence opens the side with waved, Eno-style psychedelic ambient that's ruptured by a beat isolated from Joe Delia's sordid score for Abel Ferarra's famously abhorred erotic thriller 'The Blackout'. From here, we're catapulted across Christophe Beck's 'Bring It On' soundscapes, a cloudy, sub-heavy ambient marvel from Brooklyn artist Alex Bienstock and even Joe Jackson's aborted theme for 'Mike's Murder', a 1984 Debra Winger vehicle that had its entire soundtrack replaced with a more palatable one from John Barry.

Really, we can't say enough about this one. If you've been following Scott-Anderton's mixes (if you want just one, we recommend her Krzysztof Kieślowski selection), you'll already know how vital her point of view is, but she takes us to a completely new zone with this one. It's a head-scratcher that'll have you wondering what it is yr actually listening to - a way to contemplate the Y2K era as it completely vanishes into popular mythology.

Revisiting their debut album '.After', Tujiko Noriko and Adrian Corker commission a suite of remixes, bringing in Koshiro Hino ov YPY, goat (JP) and KAKUHAN fame, Tashi Wada, DJ Trystero, Shojiro Nakaoka and DJ ojo to put their spin on the source material.

The original album only took Noriko and Corker a couple of days in the studio, but they wired the results to percussionist and arranger George Barton, who took it to the next level. They continue the thought on '.After Again', dishing out the stems to a carefully pruned list of collaborators - artists whose distinctive sounds only extend the original album's sonic universe. And of course it's the YPY version of the album's opening track 'Yasashii Sayonora' that'll have most of y'all chomping at the bit; Hino turns Corker and Noriko's source material to dust, time-stretching Noriko's vocal and zeroing in on the stuttering percussion and rusted turntable loops. Adding his signature jerks, he fills the track with clattering metallic clangs, twisting the voices into downsampled groans from a neighboring cyber-reality.

Tokyo's DJ Trystero opts for a different but similarly unique approach on his two reworks, the "All Frills" remix of 'Toku No Minato' and his "Naive Declension" version of the same track. On the former, he isolates almost indistinguishable elements of the original, setting the ghost traces to a typically deep, dubby groove and on the latter, creates a rugged, gear-heavy jam from the remains. It's actually Nakaoka who provides the weirdest - yet strangely most recognisable - versions, using his custom generative code to match Noriko's voice with whirring interference and warbling digital detritus.

items.body:
Danish producer ML Buch studies the fertile space between vintage songcraft and contemporary synthetics on 'Suntub', smudging MIDI guitar riffs and soft rock pads into acoustic instrumentation and soaring earworms. It's like Joni Mitchell's 'Hejira' or Fleetwood Mac's 'Rumours' rebuilt painstakingly by an AI-powered server farm, the edges hand-frayed into surreal, fractal patterns. A late-year contender for pop album of the year, no doubt.

As artists have spied the creeping influence of AI tools and algorithmic selection, it's caused the most perceptive among them to reconsider their craft. ML Buch takes a bold step into the known unknown on 'Suntub', playing on familiarity to force us to reckon with an uncanny reality. Her songs are rooted in an era where technology had reached a soft peak: the late-'70s/early-'80s stretch that birthed some of the most enduringly "classic" pop tomes. A confident guitarist and expressive vocalist, Buch meshes together harmonic flourishes and riffs you'll swear you've heard before, but does it in a way that sounds totally new. 

On opening track and lead single 'Pan over the hill', she uses cheap, bone-dry beatbox hits, waxy synths and sound module strings - to perch us on a queasy junction. Her guitar, processed with heavy chorus to mimic Robin Guthrie's foundational dream-pop riffing, lends a human touch, before lilting, soft-hued vocals seize the spotlight. The faded memory of trip-hop is buried in there somewhere too; Buch is a sensitive listener who acknowledges how often classic pop has been woven into the fabric of different genres, so when we hear a clunky record scratch kick, it's like a wink of acknowledgement.

Buch's vocals themselves are particularly enigmatic. She dubbed them in her Peugeot SUV, using the car as a recording booth and multi-tracking her stems to build extravagant, criss-crossing harmonic loops. It's a technique she employed on her 2020 debut album 'Skinned', and although 'Suntub' is less manifestly electronic than its predecessor, the vocals aren't completely organic, either. While Buch's voice is expressive, it's also heavily treated, shaped with Auto-Tune and various effects. It isn't anything new, sure, but Buch leans into the esoteric potential of the process, using gratifying, opulent chord and key changes to emphasize its dizzying mutability. 

At its best, 'Suntub' sounds like a pitch-perfect advancement of some of the ideas Daniel Lopatin splayed out on his last few full-lengths, particularly 'Magic Oneohtrix Point Never'. If Lopatin had wanted to recreate the sensation of listening to soft rock radio in suburban Massachusetts as a youngster, Buch responds with a more earnest, more deliberate simulacrum. The fully-reclined jazziness and forward motion of Joni Mitchell's 'Hejira' is matched with the vertiginous songwriting precision of Fleetwood Mac's 'Rumours' and its follow-up 'Tusk', and Buch swirls these inspirations into Escher-like structures, accepting how their traces have been absorbed into the collective consciousness.

On 'Flame shards goo' her vocals evanesce over glistening guitar phrases. "In the open blue, in the golden goo," she reflects, conducting a free-flowing ambient pop symphony that owes as much to Roy Montgomery as it does to Steely Dan. And although there's a brittle beat on 'Somewhere', and artificial acoustic guitar licks that remind us of Malibu's hazy post-trance deconstructions, Buch architects an idiomatic soundscape, alternating slide guitar whooshes with synthesizer wails. 

Occasionally, her advanced, nomadic DIY constructions share an intimacy with Erika de Casier, but where de Casier is singing to herself in a room filled with diaries and posters, Buch is peering through smeared glass, bellowing at the shifting clouds. Just peep 'Solid', a celestial cycle of heart-melting vocal harmonies and chugging guitars that sounds like Buch's inward world realized in 4K, sensitive but eye-poppingly vivid, as if her deepest fantasies are being brought to life in real-time. If it's dream pop, it's completely lucid, and if it's soft rock, it's been heated to gooey magma.

File next to Lee Gamble's 'Models' = highest recommendation!

items.body:
The wide-eyed, theatric art-pop and psych-folk wonders of Svitlana Nianio’s early band, Cukor Bila Smert’, come to light via Ukrainian reissue specialists Shukai on this mindboggling 31-track, 90 minute anthology of studio recordings made between 1990-1993, contorting gothic folk around brittle, calypso-inspired drum loops and oddball new wave bullets, a sort of missing link on the spectrum between Broadcast, Stroom, Lubos Fiser and Les Disques Du Crépescule.

Cukor Bila Smert’ (trans: Sugar — White Death) was a band formed by three graduates of Reinhold Glier Kyiv Academy of Music following the end of their studies in the summer of 1988. It was notably the maiden vehicle for Svitlana Nianio - then known as Svitlana Ohrimenko - with classmates Oleksandr Kohanovs’kyi and Tamila Mazur, soon to be joined by guitarist and artist Eugene Taran, who would help shape the group’s conceptual and aesthetic thrust toward enchanting forms of folk-pop psychedelia. 

As revealed here for the first time outside Ukraine, Cukor Bila Smert’ would pursue a deeply uncanny sound, at once frothy, piquant, but unsettling, and largely defined by Svitlana’s distinctive soprano, singing lyrics penned by her and Eugene Taran over delightfully rickety drum machine rhythms and tremulous, bittersweet synths and keys in a style that evokes soundtracks to imaginary Soviet cosmonaut animations or the febrile dreams of young conservatoire students readying for exams. 

The songs span some 90 minutes of music and 3 years of recordings, and are a world unto themselves, simultaneously unfurling ideas and binding you ever tighter into layers of rich, extended, storytelling melodies and skewiff harmonies that require little understanding of Ukrainian folklore in order to enjoy on their most immediate, abundant merits. We hear Svitlana’s classically trained voice puckered to all manner of instrumentation, from the purely synthetic to acoustic, in forms running from folkwise to baroque in a way that arguably parallels new age ambient, but with a more pointed, far less hippyish purpose closer to avant classical composition.

The five-part 'Six Coral Devils' is a sprawling, theatrical suite that lurches from experimental folk, bursting with hotwired strings and jerky, off-kilter piano phrases, to rickety, drum-machine-led eccentricity in the concluding segment. Turbid epic 'Argolida' (aka 'Antinoy Is Leaving') was the band’s first recording as a duo, and is split into seven pieces: 'Part III' is dissonant and freewheeling, layering doddering, fudgy guitars and creeping synth vamps beneath Nianio's otherworldly echoes, and 'Part II' comes off like a twitchy nursery rhyme, with the vocals barely a hum over juddering synths. A couple of years later, in 1992, they tackled their next album 'All Secrets of a Poem', dubbing the material in Kharkiv with Oleksandr Vakulenko. This work is been split into four pieces here, and flashes the band's lighter side with feathery vocals and punctured beatbox loops.

The final third of the anthology is taken from Nianio and Taran's final album, 'Selo' (The Village), recorded in Poland straight to reel-to-reel. With additional cello provided by session player Boleslav Blazhchyk, these tracks are an apt swan song: 'Wartowyj (The Stand Guard)' and 'Obminaj Misce (Around This Place)' and others use synthesised harpsichord to remind us of a lost past, while Nianio dances wildly with some of her most acrobatic vocal phrases. Then there's 'Procesija Mertwych (Dead Ceremony)', a fuzzy, saturated left-pop marvel that reminds us of the rattly, surrealist psych deployments Broadcast would make their signature a few short years later, and 'Na Skryni (On The Basket)' is a churning, piano-led soundscape that's blessed with punctuating breaths from Nianio. 

'Recordings 1990-1993' is a sprawling, stunning retrospective that bottles the energy of one of Ukraine's most unique and quietly revolutionary underground outfits - time to get acquainted.

items.body:
Effortlessly easy on the ear and yet still somehow fathoms-deep, Tara Clerkin Trio’s latest is their most refined and fully-formed transmission yet, mining a precious sweetspot between chamber-jazz, Plone-style bric-a-brac electronics, Crescent’s lo-fi reveries and the urban pressure of the Young Echo collective, unpicking decades of British musical history in the process. Trust, it’s a special one.

Like every great band, TCT know their history. They've grown up with and formed their identity in the shadow of Bristol's musical lore, whether it's The Pop Group, Massive Attack or Flying Saucer Attack, and when they use traceable elements, it feels like a believable part of their DNA. Thankfully, they meaningfully add to that narrative too, not adapting an aesthetic for easy consumption. Part of this might be down to their makeup; they formed in the late 20-teens from the ashes of the Tara Clerkin Band, a larger ensemble that Clerkin had put together to expand the scope of her folk-y pop compositions. And when most of the members moved on, stepbrothers Sunny-Joe Paradiso and Patrick Benjamin stuck around to see where the road might lead. All "proper" players, they've traditionally let their songs appear from what sounds like loose, casual improvisations, like you're tuned into Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society' band running through Laika's 'Silver Apples of the Moon'.

So you get a song like the brilliant 'Ups & Downs', that simmers for a good four minutes with wheezing harmonium, double bass and clarinet, percussion just rumbling in the background somewhere, before a jerky sampled beat, Mellotron strings and Clerkin's voice would have you thinking Matt Elliott's behind the boards. But 'Somewhere Good' is also remarkably tight when it needs to be, walking a tightrope between easy breezy and meticulous with acrobatic skill. Opener 'Lake Walk', for example, sounds intentionally naive, jammed out loosely on synthesised and real woodwind that's caught in a vortex of Space Echo, before 'Lazy Daisy' cuts it short with its more ordered (but still kinda slouchy) beat-heavy dreampop atmosphere. It's where the album's shape really coagulates, between Broadcast's dramatic early EPs (back when they were touring with Plone) and Pram's best shit, just lightly tweezed at the edges, its creases relaxed to fit in with Laila Sakini's quietly genius 'Paloma'. And that mood carries the record even when Clerkin's voice - pursed into a soulful croon or a lackadaisical murmur - vanishes completely. One of the most gripping moments arrives with 'There Was a Nice Sunset', effortlessly matching slowcore drums with piano flourishes and synths, locking into the same general feeling but widening the boundaries, nodding to Adrian Sherwood's lysergic work on Creation Rebel's 'Starship Africa'. 

There's years of British musical history baked into this stuff, and yet it feels wholly new.

Very different from Biosphere's last AD 93 offering, 'The Way of Time' is a freewheeling set of atmospheric vintage synth jams, dubby ambient techno experiments and decelerated electro workouts that's inspired by American poet and author Elizabeth Madox Roberts' 'The Time Of Man'. Essential listening for fans of 'Patashnik', then.

On 2021's 'Angel's Flight', Geir Jenssen focused his gaze on Beethoven's String Quartet No. 14, tweaking and stretching it to tease out its essence. He's on more familiar ground here, using Joan Lorring's voice, from a 1951 radio adaptation of 'The Time Of Man', to guide us through a spruced-up spread of his signature sounds. If you've kept up with his releases, then you'll know that the last few albums have been made with restored keyboards and drum machines - a marked shift from his period using samples and software.

'The Way Of Time' seems to follow the same path: opener 'Time Of Man' is barely more than a brassy analog lead and Lorring's smudgy voice, while the title theme (that repeats in various forms), with its acidic plucks and sequenced repetitions takes us back to Jenssen's milestone album 'Patashnik', when he set the bar for ambient techno. It's a welcome return to familiar sonics; unlike his last couple of synth-heavy albums, that sounded like fun diversions and jams, 'The Way Of Time' holds neatly together as a unit, well braided by its journeyman theme. Lorring's voice is the anchor, and Jenssen's able to refresh his most referenced material with contemporary processes and techniques.

items.body:
Anyone obsessed with those two incredible ‘Begena Songs…’ comps on Death Is Not The End will be properly enchanted by this more expansive - yet still intimate - suite of snapshots from Ethiopia, 1971, spanning the unique, twanging harp sound thru to Amharic poetry, chants, and spellbinding flute dances...

One that catches the breath with seldom felt sensations, ‘Ethiopian Musics 1971’ patently owes as much to the incredible performers as their faithful representation in Ragnar Johnson & Ralph Harrisson’s recordings. All secreted to tape on a Uher Report L stereo reel-to-reel recorder, they epitomise an era of ethnomusicological preservation, when the likes of labels such as Lyrichord and  Folkways were already decades deep “in the field”, documenting long-held traditions practically untouched by an encroaching, western modernity. And perhaps most crucially, the recordings beautifully render the acoustic settings and vivid vibes with an immersive quality in stark opposition to the era of dry, so-called audiophile studio recordings of ethnic musics to come - all the better for immersing in this wonderfully unfamiliar world.

The abundance of singular tones and strong, rare feels they produce is quite staggering to our northern english ears, and we reckon also for anyone else, for that matter. Opening to a joyful couplet of a bluesy ’Song about the beauty of women’, and the almost shanty-like swing and hard rhythm of ’Tej Beit Song’, the set reels to distinctive pieces of Ethiopian Christian song set to begena, or ‘Harp of David’, buzz, and a landscape-scale, 13 minute ‘Love Song (Mary Armede)’. A gripping ‘Drum Song (Jigsaw)’ will be mana to rhythm fiends, and a number of standout flute pieces reprise the frisson of our first encounter with this discipline on Sublime Freq’s ‘Staring into the Sun - Ethiopian Tribal Music’ set of 2012, most potently on the pluming twin pipes of the ‘Fila Flute Dance’ parts, whilst the pentatonic craar (6-stringed lyre) parts surely strike nerves for lovers of the rawest blues, and hail the liberated legacy of Mary Armede, a folk singer-fashion designer of Azmari heritage who surely warrants further investigation. 

No doubt this is one of the most striking archival discoveries of 2026, acutely advised to anyone enchanted with music from this corner of the world from Éthiopiques to begena harp, thru to Ragnar Johnson’s other arenas of research for Ideologic Organ in Yemen or Papua New Guinea. Dive in without delay.

An iconic album originally brought to life via Sweden's peerless iDEAL Recordings, Kali Malone’s 'The Sacrificial Code’ is a major work featuring almost two hours of concentrated, creeping organ pieces aligned to non traditional intonation/tuning systems. It's a stunning realisation of ideas borne out of academic and conceptual rigour, with a perception-altering quality that encourages exploration without a preordained endpoint.

The Sacrificial Code’ takes a more surgical approach to the methods first explored on last year’s ‘Organ Dirges 2016 - 2017’. Over the course of three parts performed on three different organs, Malone’s minimalist process captures a jarring precision of closeness, both on the level of the materiality of the sounds and on the level of composition.The recordings here involved careful close miking of the pipe organ in such a way as to eliminate environmental identifiers as far as possible - essentially removing the large hall reverb so inextricably linked to the instrument. The pieces were then further compositionally stripped of gestural adornments and spontaneous expressive impulse -  an approach that flows against the grain of the prevailing musical hegemony, where sound is so often manipulated, and composition often steeped in self indulgence. It echoes Steve Reich’s sentiment “..by voluntarily giving up the freedom to do whatever momentarily comes to mind, we are, as a result, free of all that momentarily comes to mind.”

With its slow, purified and seemingly austere qualities ‘The Sacrificial Code’ guides us through an almost trance-inducing process where we become vulnerable receptors for every slight movement, where every miniature shift in sound becomes magnified through stillness. As such, it’s a uniquely satisfying exercise in transcendence through self restraint and by this point inarguably a modern classic.

Void Control continues to explore the relationship between rhythm, space, and low-frequency energy.

"Each track is built around movement and atmosphere, combining organic percussion, spacious dub textures, and weighty sub frequencies.

Drawing influence from reggae sound system culture, tribal rhythms, dub techno, and contemporary bass music, the release exists at the intersection of multiple underground traditions. Rather than treating these influences as separate genres, Void Control allows them to interact naturally, creating a cross-pollination of sounds that feels both familiar and forward-thinking."

items.body:
Old pals Christina Vantzou and Félicia Atkinson reflect on coastal living on their first collaborative album, blending environmental echoes from Rome, Normandy and Hydra with mellow synth, piano, Rhodes, vibraphone, lap steel, gongs and spoken word, pulling us into the sublime.

The third chapter in RVNG's ongoing "Reflections" series, 'Water Poems' crystallises a creative relationship that began way back in 2009. Vantzou and Atkinson have performed together before, most notably in 2019 at Philharmonie de Paris, but this is the first time the duo have made a record together. Both artists live by the sea, Atkinson in Normandy on the French coast, and Vantzou in Greece, using that shared experience to power a series of hazy dream sequences filled with subtle gestures. "The sea was not taken as a monolithic postcard," Atkinson explains. "But more of a person; an energy, a mystery, a complex character we face everyday, as human beings living by the sea."

Indeed, the esoteric energy of the sea - its tides, force, majesty and hypnotic, mystical pull, is captured by the duo's eddy of electroacoustic treatments and bespoke natural soundscapes. They recorded the material in a factory on the island of Hydra in Greece, at Villa Medici in Rome and at home in their respective studios, adding expressive environmental recordings from Delphi and the Eftalou Hot Springs. The record plays like a single, hazed thought, ebbing and flowing through the same shallow waters. Words emerge and disappear into carefully processed sounds at first, before forming sentences and whole thoughts on the second side. "How can a body swim," Atkinson mouthes. "How can a person dream?"

Gorgeously, quietly seductive gear from two of the very best at this sort of thing, one to file next to Meitei's sublime 'Sen'nyū (泉涌)' from last year - recline and drift into it.

Still influential three decades after its release, Rachel's' debut album is a low-key genre classic, welding the cinematic orchestrations of Carter Burwell to nascent post-rock structures and influencing bands like A Silver Mt. Zion and Clogs in the process.

Originally deployed on Touch And Go's sister label Quaterstick in 1995, 'Handwriting' was a complete anomaly at the time. There was a feeling that the album had only appeared on the label because it'd been the home of Rodan, the popular post-hardcore outfit that Rachel's founder Jason Noble had been a member of. But as time ticked on, Rachel's forward-thinking fusion of post-rock and chamber music began to appear more prescient. The band was originally conceived by Noble and viola player Christian Frederickson in the late '80s, but when Rodan blew up, Noble was too preoccupied to follow up their experiments. Time, of course, ticked on and Rodan imploded, so Noble and Frederickson picked up the pieces, inviting pianist Rachel Grimes to contribute. And the band's debut is a real one-off; they'd follow it with the brilliant Nyman-esque 'Music for Egon Schiele', but by that time their post-hardcore/post-rock echoes had all but disappeared. As it is, 'Handwriting' is at the root of a sound that almost immediately blossomed further north in Montréal. 

Linking the tangled riffs of Slint and of course Rodan with the scenic ambience of Labradford and, most importantly, Michael Nyman's minimal compositions, Noble, Grimes and Frederickson pre-empted something that's permeated throughout the scene at large over the three decades that followed. Even 'M. Daguerre', one of the album's early highlights and its jazziest track, that hews closer to The Necks' early material than anything else, provides a tangible blueprint. But it's the cooler, quieter moments that keep us coming back to 'Handwriting', like the emotive 'Seratonin' or the absolute milestone 'Full on Night', a stripped-to-the-bone Southern gothic post-rock jam that dissolves into a mass of radio static, film samples and chugging steam trains. If Godspeed hadn't heard this one before they recorded 'F♯ A♯ ∞', we'd be very surprised.

Recorded in 1991, 'Rise' sweeps up all known recorded material from A.R. Kane's Rudy Tambala and Cranes vocalist Alison Shaw, aka inrain, compiling a classic 7” for Rough Trade with additional, previously unreleased tracks. It’ll no doubt provide many with a first introduction to a prescient project by two scene legends, delving into shoegaze, dub, electro and trip-hop refractions of the highest order. It's the most essential Music From Memory release in a hot minute, crucial listening for all A.R Kane obsessives (that should be all of you) or anyone into Seefeel, Locust, Zurich.

For someone for whom Cranes' ‘Tomorrow's Tears’ and A.R Kane’s ‘Lolita’ are two absolute foundational texts, this reissue is basically something like a holy grail. Back in 1991, inrain appeared on Rough Trade's Singles Club series with a brief but brilliant 7" that sounded as if it'd been beamed in from another planet. A.R. Kane had already broken the mold, but these three tracks juxtaposed Shaw's dreamy vocals with dubby, spacious electronics and shimmering guitars in a way that wouldn't really rise to prominence until years later. Music From Memory do the heavy lifting here, remastering that original 7" from the original DAT tapes and adding the extra track 'Biology' and an alternate version of 'Sleep' to bump up the package. 

It's those original tracks that have us by the throat - we really can't believe they've been so slept on over the years. '...And Julie Rose' sounds like it should have been picked up for a Duophonic release a decade later, while 'Sleep' completely pre-empts Seefeel's 'More Like Space EP' that wouldn't appear for another couple of years. 

Prophetic, brilliant stuff.

Piano Works 2016-2026 collects fourteen impromptu pieces by composer and producer John Carroll Kirby, written whenever he had the opportunity to sit at a piano while on the road.

"These mostly solo works for piano were recorded in Los Angeles, Rome, Tokyo, Wollongong (Australia), rural New Zealand and London.

Piano Works marks a departure from the full-band sound of recent albums Blowout and Septet, which Kirby has spent the past years performing live around the world. The album is a study in piano repertoire: Baroque, Romantic, Impressionist, jazz, minimalist, atonal, and more. Most of the pieces have an impromptu feel – improvised, or meant to sound improvised, or at least written in one sitting.

The collected pieces on Piano Works are a document of Kirby’s life as a piano player and touring musician, and “serve as the melodic / harmonic lexicon for what would inform all my other compositions of the past ten years.”

items.body:
The Sultans of Sludge slang a definitive label debut for Sub Pop, bringing their singular sound to roost on a legendary label local to their origins in the US north west, whose rugged landscapes fed directly into the LP’s formidably primal concentration of dualistic energies

Hailing some 30 years since Sunn O)))’s formation, their eponymous 10th studio album reckons with forces of nature - time and space, dark and light - for 80 minutes of air-shuddering pressure limning epic, craggy vistas from a thick haar of distortion. Subtly enlivened with field recordings made in forests near Bear Creek Studios, Woodinville, Washington, where O’Malley says they would “go hiking and be out in the woods, spend time outdoors”, the resulting six-part sequence sees the duo drill down to fundamentals with an absorbing sense of purpose and telepathically-attuned intuition. A notable dearth of other contributors also means it’s one of their truest statements as a duo; just Stephen O’Malley & Greg Anderson howling into the wilds on all instrumentation, from trusted axes to keys and electro-acoustic sorcery. 

At this point, not to labour the arboreal metaphors, but it may take a certified guide to see the wood for the trees in Sunn O))) lands, such is the uniquely coherent sprawl of their sound at 30 years up to the hilt in atonal rock doom. Our hair’s not long enough to lay claim as spirit guides, but after 23 years of bearing witness to them live, and ingesting most of their LPs, we can say this side is wholly emblematic of their radical steez. Between the two 18 minute totems of a ‘XXANN’ laced with location recording of running water at tender points, and a ‘Mindrolling’ monstered with claw-handed riffs, they take it to typically stare-down levels of intensity with the sustained threat of ‘Does Anyone Hear Like Venom?’, and billowing sheets of subharmonic distortion harnessed in ‘Everett Moses’. Closer ‘Glory Black’ is, however, a sort of sore thumb with a relatively conventional riff progression and rising banks of silvery wheeze that collapse into keys and field recordings, hearkening most closely to the duo’s precedents and NW peers in the Sub Pop roster, Earth, or even another touchstone, Black Sabbath, at their most strung out. 

Heavy as your life.

I can feel the waves is Frances Chang's debut on RVNG Intl.

"A boundary-pushing musician and multi-media artist from Brooklyn, New York, Frances Chang disrupts accepted reality through her unique and enchanting compositions. Chang’s songs are an exercise in communication, probing the tension between idiosyncratic personal experience and the drive to understand, and be understood, through a collective language.

For “I can feel the waves,” a piano-centric melody is ornamented with primitive electronics and poetic vocals. The track boldly demonstrates Chang’s strength for unconventional yet contagious songwriting, and pioneers a genre the artist refers to as “slacker prog”: roomy and playful, offbeat and occasionally jarring, brimming with spiritual and emotional resonance.

The b-side, “Marry,” is a rollicking yet laid-back composition, with undaunted wobbly kicks bubbling under pianistic textures until a dialogue, acted out between Chang and Sylvia Gorelick, takes the foreground in the final moments of the track. As the instrumental carries its freewheeling pulse forward, the conversation, inspired by films like Kenneth Lonergan’s Margaret and Catherine Breillat’s Fat Girl!, along with Broken Social Scene’s “Anthems for a Seventeen-Year Old Girl,” turns toward the relationship between internal subjectivity and the external necessity of “staying small.”

Where is Frances headed from here? A piano is at the center, synths and strings swelling around its shoulders. A little less tension, a lot more production. Some shadows will be encountered, some forgotten skeletons unearthed. Music excavated from the subtler, deeper layers of cerebral and shared experiences. Music that is truly its own."

New album by acclaimed Nigerian ambient producer / sound designer Ibukun Sunday, interweaving Africanised rhythm with lush and elegant synthesis.

"Ibukun Sunday follows his acclaimed debut Harmony / Balance with Olúsín [Worshippers], an album exploring faith through ambient composition and West African musical traditions. Inspired by devotional practices, it combines subtle percussion, vocal harmonies and spacious electronics to evoke both communal worship and quiet reflection.

Born in Lagos and now based in north London, Sunday draws on field recordings, minimalist motifs and his background as a classically trained violist to create music that is understated yet emotionally resonant.

Jeff McIlwain re-emerges from his production slumber to deliver more aural candy for the Ghostly family on this new Lusine album.

Further settling into his latter-day groove as a producer of well-polished pop-tinged electronics, the Lusine of nearly 20 years ago has not disappeared altogether, the mechanics of his early IDM, ambient and downtempo productions still drive the creative process on ‘Sensorimotor’.

There is a more introspective yearn to this album however, a sensation most apparent in the numerous vocal contributions from Jeff and his wife, Sarah McIlwain, along with Vilja Larjosto and Benoît Pioulard. The latter’s manipulated vocals feature on the sub-Burial, hushed flutter of Witness which is destined to get synced by the CSI franchise sometime soon.

Dead sturdy, darkside D&B shadow-boxers and rollers by the Bristol don, on his first solo mission of ’26 and back on home turf with his UVB-76 Music crew.

After moonlighting, in recent years, on a more raved-up EP with Ilian Tape, and his ’93-style hardcore bullets wth AD 93, Kristian Jabs aka Pessimist slips back into baddest D&B habits on the ‘Pony Boy Cub EP’. 

The A-side locks off a signature strip of dread martial steppers tension in ‘Pess One’, pivoting ghoulish bass spectres around flintiest snares harking to his aces for BEB/A14, next to the drily ricocheting drums and halftime rolige of a title tune reminding of his input to the Ruffhouse trio with Karim Maas & Vega. 

His B-side gets ruder with the pugilist drums on ‘NRG-97’, swarmed with string stabs and voice-in-head motifs recalling SD’s ‘Technical Warfare’ and Boymerang missiles, and coming with the strongback crud in a properly cantankerous ‘Under Surveillance’.

items.body:
Jospehine Foster's 2016 release "No More Lamps In the Morning" available again via Fire Records.

"Foster, on nylon string guitar, and husband Victor Herrero, accompanying on Portuguese guitar, together weave intimate readings of songs spanning Foster's songwriting career including selections from recent albums "This Coming Gladness" (2008) and "I'm a Dreamer" (2013) and back to Born Heller (2004). Foster's new route is a free, chromatic music, a tuneful montana of mind--an expansive harmonic space dominated by Rif mountain on the horizon. As highwater as the music is, as broad the stylistic palette of the musicians, the music really exists in service of the lyrics. Two of the songs on No More Lamps are poems by Rudyard Kipling and James Joyce given musical settings by Foster. The rest arguably are musical settings of her own poems strengthened in a fiery crucible of guitars (and on 2 tracks Gyða Valtýsdóttir's cello) in which dissonant notes bend and quaver as wirefork embers, dying without affecting the glowing tonal fire which unites contrary forces in a Moroccan speakeasy. She and Herrero have performed, for an audience of burros, concerts of Federico Garcia Lorca poems set to music. A music of wandering and a music of roots."

items.body:
The Original Motion Picture Soundtrack for Crime 101 by experimental electronic musician, producer and composer Blanck Mass (She Rides Shotgun).

"Thunderous synth soundscapes are paired with nuanced character-driven themes creating a multi-faceted backdrop to the intense thriller. The Amazon MGM Studios film directed by Bart Layton is set against the sun-bleached grit of Los Angeles.

Crime 101 weaves the tale of an elusive jewel thief (Chris Hemsworth) whose string of heists along the 101 freeway have mystified police. When he eyes the score of a lifetime, his path crosses that of a disillusioned insurance broker (Halle Berry) who is facing her own crossroads. Convinced he has found a pattern, a relentless detective (Mark Ruffalo) is closing in, raising the stakes even higher. As the heist approaches, the line between hunter and hunted begins to blur, and all three are faced with life-defining choices– and the realization that there can be no turning back.

On creating the music, Power says :

“Crime 101 was an incredible movie to have the opportunity to score. At the centre of the story is, of course, the heist. However, it very quickly became apparent to me that this was not any heist movie, but more a Noir which happens to have a heist in it. The central characters and how their lives become intertwined was more important than the action, in a way. This is high-octane in parts, of course, but what really drew me to this movie was the character development. Lou, Davis and Sharon are the beating heart. I wanted to ‘be with them sonically’ throughout. Both the tender and the furious needed to be sympathetic with one another”."
